chapters.headline: The invisible hit: the record-breaking No. 1 nobody you know has heard
Watch Lanterns before it becomes a movie footnote

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Hi, hello. Mikey Okada is here, which means the normal-person level in this room just went way up.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Hi. That's the nicest way anyone's ever called me boring.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: It's the highest compliment I have. I mean it.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: You sent me a voice memo at twelve-forty last night.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I did. That was research!

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: It sounded like a hostage tape.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ha. Okay, it was a little bit of a hostage tape.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Did you eat dinner at any point during this research?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I had crackers. Over the sink.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Christina.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Fancy crackers! They had rosemary in them.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Oh, rosemary. Sorry, I didn't realize it was a dinner party. Wait, hold on. I heard you on the Builder show with Bea. You were going to deal with that email. The offer one.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: ...You listen to the Builder show?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: I listen to everything. I don't have a group chat. Did you answer it?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I wrote a reply.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Nice!

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And I sent it to myself.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Ha. Oh no.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: It's in my inbox right now, looking up at me. It's progress! It moved one inbox over.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Does Bea know?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Bea's going to find out when she hears this, so, hi Bea. Can we please talk about a song now?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Yes. The humming song.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: The humming song. I was trying to hum the biggest song in America and I couldn't get past the first line. "Choosin' Texas." Ella Langley. It just passed "All I Want for Christmas Is You" for the most weeks at number one ever.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Which is a song that has an entire season working for it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: It has December on the payroll! And this song beat it, and the reaction from basically everyone I read was confusion. Who is this, where did it come from?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: CNN had to run an explainer, right? And the explanation was the algorithm. Everybody's in their own little feed, so nobody shares a song anymore.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And I think that's backwards. If feeds broke the hit into a million pieces, number ones would get weaker. Shorter stays, more churn. This one has more weeks on top than anything in the chart's history. Fragmentation doesn't make that.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Mm.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So here's my read. The hit is huge. The part that splintered is the little group of people who decide what counts as culture. And we mostly don't live where this song is on in the truck.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: "We."

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Me! I mean me. Okay, I'm too online, but I can at least see the outline of my own blind spot.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Can you, though?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: ...Some days. Tuesdays.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Who are you fighting with on this? Somebody's gotta be on the other side.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Two people. First, Ryan Broderick, who writes the Garbage Day newsletter. He went down every song that's ever held this record, and the only one he'd never heard, other than this one, was Morgan Wallen's "Last Night."

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Also country.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Also country. He flags that. But his explanation is the industry. In January all the Christmas songs fall off the streaming chart, there's a big hole, and Nashville pushed this song into it with radio.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: See, I kind of believe him. Sorry.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: The second one is Chuck Klosterman, and he's about critics versus the charts. Park him, I'm coming back for him.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Parked.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So, the push. I think it's the least interesting part. Argue with me.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Okay. Stay with me here. There's a guy at the bar, sits at the far end, and every night he puts the same song on the jukebox. Same one, over and over. If you pulled the jukebox numbers, that song is the biggest hit in the building. Not close.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: What's the song?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: I'm not saying. He'd find out. Point is, ask anybody else in there to hum it. Nobody can. The bartender can't stand it, but he only cares about the over/under, so he lets it ride.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ha.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: So that's my worry. The chart counts plays now, and plays reward the guy at the end of the bar. A group that loves one song a lot can sit on top for months while the rest of the room never learns the words. That's a narrower hit than Mariah. Smaller footprint, deeper hole.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: That's a great image. I think it's wrong for this song.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Go.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Radio. Your guy can stream it all night. He can't make radio play it. And radio keeps playing it. People in cars and kitchens and dentist's offices heard it without ever picking it.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Okay. That's a lot of guys at the end of a lot of bars.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: That's every bar!

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: But hang on. Radio is a machine too. Somebody in an office decided to play it. That's Broderick's whole point, and you just told me you don't care about it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I care! I just think every hit has a machine. Mariah has a machine. It's called Christmas.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Ha. Okay.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Radio pushing a country song is how country songs have always become hits. Nobody called Garth a fake hit because radio played him.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Fair. Here's the part that bugs me more, though. If this record keeps falling, isn't it kind of inflated? Like home runs in a certain era.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ooh.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Streaming's sticky. People don't move on, the playlists just keep running. So twenty-four weeks now might be worth, I don't know, twelve in 1995.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, that's the best argument against me and I hate it.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: But it cuts my way too. If the shared hit were dying, why are the biggest runs in history all from the last few years? "Old Town Road." "Despacito."

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Shaboozey.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Shaboozey! "A Bar Song" had the record right before this one, if you take out Mariah's Christmas bump. Did everybody hear "A Bar Song"?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Everybody heard "A Bar Song." My mom heard "A Bar Song."

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Did everybody hear it? Or did we hear it, because it got into our feeds as a meme?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: ...Oh, that's annoying.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Right? Two songs, pretty close in sound, a lot of the same listeners. One went viral with people like us and one didn't. And we decided the first one was a big shared moment and the second one needs an explainer.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Yeah. I don't have an answer for that. I'm gonna sit with it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, history bit, and I'm saying up front it's one example.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Disclaimer noted.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Think about country when Garth Brooks showed up. The people who covered music lost their minds.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: And people lost their minds.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: The people who covered music lost their minds. The people buying it weren't surprised at all. They'd been buying it the whole time! These are the same story, 1991 and this week. The audience was always there, and the people looking were standing somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: I like it. I don't trust it, but I like it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Why don't you trust it?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Because in '91 nobody could see those people. The count was broken. Now the count's great. The radio numbers are sitting right there in public. Anybody could look.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: That's my point! ...Yeah. Okay. That's a lot worse, actually.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Sorry.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: No, you're right. I turned it into a measurement story so it would be nobody's fault. And that one's on us. On me.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: And I'll give you one back. I came in buying the January push. But a trick gets you a week, right? It got knocked off in the spring and climbed back up and stayed all summer.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: It came back!

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Nobody pushes a song back to the top in July. People went back to it. So I moved. A little.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, unparking Klosterman. The idea that critics and the charts have drifted together. I think he's half right.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Hasn't it kind of happened, though? Critics love pop now. Nobody's sneering at Taylor Swift.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: They love the pop they can see. He's right about the part of the map critics actually visit. This is the biggest song in the country by the oldest measure we've got, and the press response was an explainer.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: So the gap closed, except in the parts of the country they don't drive through.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Yes. That's my whole disagreement with him, right there.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Did you ask anybody normal? Outside your phone?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I texted my brother. Dev, he's a nurse in Chicago, he doesn't have a single app I write about. I asked if he'd heard "Choosin' Texas." He wrote back in a minute: yes, it's on in the break room constantly.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Of course it is.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And then a second text. Just: "why?"

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Ha!

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: That's his thing. Whatever I send him, he wants to know what it's for. I didn't have a great answer.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: My dad would know it too, I bet. Radio's always on in that kitchen. He's never once asked me what's trending.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Your dad and Dev should start a podcast.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Nobody would hear about it and it'd be number one for six months.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ha! And honestly, Tom, that's your clients. The feed they live in is a sample, and a small one. When somebody says "nobody's talking about it," that tells you who's talking. So when a brand says it wants to be big, ask which big. Reach with a huge audience that doesn't post, or buzz with the people who do. Those used to come together. Now you buy them separately.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Check the brief against the radio numbers.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Against the radio numbers! In 2026. Who knew. Okay, I'll put a bet down. December, when all the big best-songs-of-the-year lists come out. Take the five songs that show up on the most lists. Zero of them will be songs that got played on country radio.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Zero? Not one?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Zero.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: I'll take that. One sneaks in. Somebody puts a country song on there to look brave.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Loser buys dinner at your bar.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Deal. Wait. Are you making one of those lists?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: ...I'm making one of those lists.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: So you could just not put one on yours.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Or I could put one on mine and lose on purpose because I'm a person of integrity. Oh no.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Here's where I'm still stuck, though. Radio, fine, I'll give you reach. But to me shared culture is a wedding. A song comes on and the whole room sings. Your aunt, the bride's college roommate, the DJ. If half that room can't hum it, that's a big hit in a small room. I'm not sure it belongs to everybody.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Half the room can hum it, though. My half can't.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Then that's two rooms.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Or it's one room and I'm standing by the coat check.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Ha. No. I think it's two rooms. I think two rooms is the actual news.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And I think the record says it's one room and we picked bad seats. We're not settling this.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Nope. Never.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Okay, give me the pick. Please let it involve a cape. I need my comfort zone after that.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: It has a ring, which is close. Lanterns. The whole first season's on HBO Max now that the finale's out.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Oh, good.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And the finale hands John Stewart over to the Superman sequel. So watch it now, while it's still a show.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Ominous.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: A little. If the studio treats the show as the audition and the movie as the job, that tells you what they think the real product is. Everything weekly TV is good at gets filed under warm-up.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: And weekly's the thing that made Aaron Pierre.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Aaron Pierre is a different name now than he was a couple of months ago. And it happened week by week. You meet him, every week you get a little more used to having him around, and then one day he's just a star.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: That's my whole religion. The kid who looks lost in November and different in March. You only get that if you show up every week. A movie hands you the finished guy in two hours and says, here, love him.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Right. Weekly makes you wait together, and the waiting is where you get attached.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: And Kyle Chandler's in it, which, come on.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Kyle Chandler walks in and you trust him in four seconds. He's been building that for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: He's the dad you'd want yelling at the refs.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ha. Is yours still doing the two languages?

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Both languages. My mom says the refs can't hear him in either one.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ha!

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: But see, I came in ready to mourn it too. What if it goes the other way? John Stewart shows up in a giant movie, a bunch of people go, wait, who is this guy, and they go back and find the show.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Hm.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Okay, that's the optimism talking.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: No, some of them will. I'll give you that. The movie could be a door back in.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: But the people who come through that door are watching a guy they already know becomes a star. Every scene where he's unsure of himself, they've seen the poster.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: ...Ugh. Yeah. That's scouting a player off his highlight reel.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So I'd still watch it now, before the movie tells you how to feel about him.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: And I'll still bet the movie sends people back.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: To a show where they already know the ending. Fine. We'll see. That's the pick: Lanterns, season one. And then go ask somebody outside your feed what's playing in their break room.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: And eat a real dinner.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I'll eat a real dinner. And I'll send the email. To someone other than me.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: I'm telling Bea you said that.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: She already heard. Thanks, Mikey.

transcript.speaker: mikey
transcript.text: Bye, Tom. Bye, rosemary crackers.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Bye!
